why.Southern line via the Aasgard-side slope: When the lake outlet crossing looks unreasonable; it avoids the ford but means a brushy bushwhack and a gully that can hold snow into early summer, so it takes longer.

review.notes: Reports confirm the outlet path as the quick, usual way; the southern gully is not described online, so the reason rests on the stored notes.
fromStoredNotes: Southern line via the Aasgard-side slopes and the leftmost gully

why.Colchuck Lake, bare-ice glacier (late se: Late summer, when the glacier has melted to hard ice; needs crampons, often two tools, and a down-climb because the snow glissade is gone, so most parties prefer the early window.

review.notes: Several reports call early to mid season best and late season icy and difficult. Same walk-in; the two entries are seasonal conditions.

why.Early-season snow to the notch: Early in the season, once the highway reopens and before the gully melts out; it needs an axe and perhaps crampons, but the rock stays frozen in place and rockfall is lower.

review.notes: Guides agree the gully stays snow filled and can be icy until late June; this is the same line in different conditions.

why.Phelps Creek over Spider Gap: When the Lake Chelan ferry and Holden shuttle are not running; far longer, with a steep snow climb to Spider Gap, so it suits strong parties who can commit to a multi-day trip.

review.notes: Copper Creek from Holden is the standard way in; Spider Gap is the other way to reach Holden by foot. The stored primary agrees.

why.Devils Dome loop from the East Bank trai: When the Canyon Creek ford looks too risky, as in spring or early summer; it trades the day trip for a roughly 48-mile, three-day loop over Devils Dome.

review.notes: Canyon Creek trailhead is the common way in; recent reports describe the ford as usually mild by midsummer, so the loop is a high-water or access choice.

why.Big Beaver valley and Wiley Ridge: When avoiding the Hannegan route's cable-car crossing and the long loss and regain of height near Whatcom Pass; a boat ride and an easy trail lead to a steep Wiley Ridge bushwhack, over several days.

review.notes: Stored data marks Hannegan and Whatcom Pass as primary; reports describe Wiley Ridge as a longer, flatter-then-brushy alternative for the Challenger and Picket area.

why.Crest trail to Hemlock Camp and the nort: To skip the thick Swamp Creek brush on easier forest slopes, though recent beetle deadfall at the old camp and on the climb to the col slows the steep start and makes it less attractive.

review.notes: Swamp Creek is still called standard despite the brush. A recent report says Hemlock Camp is gone and the col climb is choked with deadfall.

problems: The Hemlock Camp entry's notes call it the better choice and substantially easier, but a recent trip report says the camp no longer exists and the climb to the col is blocked by deadfall. Its notes may be out of date.

why.From the Chilliwack Lake road on the Can: For parties already in Canada, as it is a much shorter walk to the saddle camp, but it crosses the border on foot away from a port of entry and is not a lawful way in for everyone.

review.notes: Reports confirm Hannegan Pass as the route that avoids legal issues and the Canadian approach as shorter but overgrown. Primary stays the Hannegan route.

problems: The Canadian-side way in crosses the border off a port of entry; owner may wish to review whether it should be listed at all.

why.Ptarmigan Traverse from Cascade Pass: When Dome is reached as part of the whole Ptarmigan Traverse, camping at White Rock Lakes; it is much longer and needs glacier skills, so it is not chosen for Dome alone.

review.notes: Downey and Bachelor Creek is the shorter, more common way; the Ptarmigan Traverse is the long, scenic option. Note that the Suiattle River Road was closed west of Downey Creek after the 2020 fire.

why.Standup Creek trail: For a quieter, gentler start from the Standup Creek side, or when making a loop that crosses the ridge between the two creeks, with the hard climbing saved for the upper slopes.

review.notes: Both valleys are used and well reported; the route is named for the southwest ridge reached from Earl Pass via Bean Creek, so the stored primary stands, though Standup is also popular.

why.From Stehekin up Agnes and Spruce Creeks: When coming from Stehekin by boat or floatplane, or linking with Dome and the Gunsights; a long trail then brush to the Icy-Spruce col, instead of the Downey Creek approach.

review.notes: Reports show Downey and Itswoot Ridge as the usual way in; the Agnes-Spruce route is described as a possibly better but slower-to-reach option.

why.Camping at the lake below the ridge: When splitting the climb over two days, with a comfortable camp and reliable water in the lake meadows below the ridge.

review.notes: Reports say most parties reach the East Ridge via Kindy Creek and camp near Cyclone Lake, so the second entry is a camp, not a route.
fromStoredNotes: Camping at the lake below the ridge

problems: 'Camping at the lake below the ridge' is a camping note on the same ground, not a separate way in; consider removing it from the ways-in list.
